faqs.q: Something is digging up my Camden lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

The homes here sit in Sandhills horse country and pine woods west of the Wateree River swamps, with Columbia suburbs at Lugoff and Elgin, and that habitat explains most of what we find: raccoons, gray squirrels, fox squirrels, armadillos account for the bulk of our Camden calls, moving between the wild ground and the housing along the same creeks, field edges, and canopy streets every night.

Antebellum and early-1900s homes in Camden, newer subdivisions in Lugoff and Elgin, and farmhouses on sandy lots. In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Every Camden job starts with a full inspection of the roofline, foundation, and crawlspace, and ends with the entries sealed — because in Kershaw County there is always another animal nearby ready to use an open hole.

faqs.q: We keep finding snakes around our Lugoff house. What can be done?
faqs.a: Most snakes we are called about in Lugoff are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs around Wateree River-side suburbs and creek woods west of Camden. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and the cottonmouth around wet ground, swamp edges, and pond banks. Identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, note where it went, and call us. Venomous snakes are safety-and-identification work, not a guaranteed capture, and the lasting fix is usually habitat — clearing brush, woodpiles, and rodent shelter near the house. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is referral-only — it is never handled as a removal job.

faqs.q: We found an opossum in our Lugoff crawlspace. What happens next?
faqs.a: In Lugoff, opossums move into crawlspaces through broken vents and loose doors, then rotate dens every few days, which is why sightings come and go. We trap at the access point, remove the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and seal the full foundation line. Securing pet food and trash at night removes the other half of the attraction.

faqs.q: What affects how big a removal job in Lugoff is?
faqs.a: Three things drive a Lugoff job: the species, the structure, and the season. Species decides the method — exclusion for bats, trapping and sealing for raccoons and skunks. Structure decides the labor, since older housing near Wateree River-side suburbs and creek woods west of Camden often hides several entries behind additions and repairs. Season decides the timing, especially when litters or bat pups mean part of the work waits a few weeks. You get the full picture from the inspection before committing to the plan.

Elgin.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Elgin and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the Sandhills subdivisions and pine stands toward the Richland line. Homeowners here phone us first about opossums under farmhouses, then about bats in older gables and church rooflines.

Small-town housing here mixes antebellum-era homes near the center with farmhouses and newer builds along the highways, nearly all with vented crawlspaces. Deep sand changes everything here: burrows hold their shape, armadillos and skunks dig easily, and longleaf pine woods press right up against farmyards and small-town lots.

Before we leave a Elgin home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: There are bats in my Bethune attic. When can they be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are excluded, never trapped or killed, and South Carolina requires no permit to remove them. Timing follows SCDNR guidance rather than a state ban: complete exclusions are scheduled for early spring (March–April) or late summer into fall (August–October), because excluding in May through mid-July can trap flightless pups inside. In Bethune we fit one-way exits over the entry points used by colonies near Lynches River farm and timber country in the county's east, seal every other gap of 3/8 inch or more, and clean guano once the colony is out. A single bat found in living quarters is different — do not handle it, and it should go to the SC Department of Public Health for rabies testing.

faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a Bethune job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near Lynches River farm and timber country in the county's east with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. Bethune.wildlife_intro:
The pattern in Bethune is set by the Lynches River farm and timber country in the county's east. If we had to name this town's signature jobs, they would be gray squirrels in pecan and oak shade trees and raccoons following creek bottoms.

Older farmhouses on pier foundations, small-town brick homes from the early 1900s, and scattered mobile homes on sandy lots make up most of the housing, with outbuildings on nearly every property. Between the pine stands and the creek bottoms, animals commute along fence rows and field drains, and sandy soil means a burrow opened one week is occupied again the next unless it is screened shut.

Every job in Bethune ends the same way it should: openings found on the inspection closed in steel mesh and flashing, so the house near Lynches River farm and timber country in the county's east stops advertising vacancies to the next animal that passes.
